brief.head: Age brings judgment
brief.text: Memory, prob­lem-solving and even cre­ativ­ity peak in youth and mid­dle age, Ajay Shah said. Age brings judg­ment: the spidey sense that a pawn storm is com­ing. {094-C05}

brief.head: An expert’s panic
brief.text: Before record­ing the episode on rules rather than dis­cre­tion, Shah woke in a panic: had he missed some­thing since his PhD days? He hadn’t, but val­ues the nerves. {094-S03}

brief.head: The last hot chocolate
brief.text: A friend taught Shah to pause and imag­ine: this is the last time I will do this. Suddenly the mo­ment changes colour, and comes to life. {094-C10}

brief.head: One book to die for
brief.text: Torn be­tween book ideas, a friend got one ques­tion from Amit Varma: if you had one book in you and would die after it, which? He wrote an­other. {094-S04}

brief.head: Messi’s second skin
brief.text: You can­not copy Messi’s style, Varma told a crew mem­ber. Messi starts with love, drills the ba­sics daily, and his ge­nius sits on top like a skin. {094-C08}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah read the wise side of Twitter
lead.head: Twelve tweets to live by

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 94

body: Amit Varma keeps a folder of tweets he calls Good Gyan. In the sec­ond episode built on it, he read twelve to Ajay Shah, and the two talked over what each was worth.
It began with John Coltrane: “You can play a shoe­string if you’re sin­cere.” Varma aimed it at peo­ple who say they can­not af­ford a good gui­tar, or own only a phone cam­era. {094-C01}
William Shakespeare, Varma said, did not refuse to write for want of a lap­top. “He found a quill from some­where.”
## Comfort and great­ness

Greg Isenberg’s tweet was five words long: great­ness and com­fort rarely co­ex­ist. Varma, who calls him­self an ex­treme in­tro­vert, started his pod­cast any­way, and hated how he looked on cam­era in the show’s early episodes. “But I just bar­reled through,” he said. {094-S02}
Shah urged com­fort with phys­i­cal dis­com­fort: dingy ho­tels, hard travel, bad food. Varma’s caveat: wor­ry­ing about next month’s rent is a real cog­ni­tive bur­den.

Neither host would fetishise the sprint. The lives of Newton and Einstein, Shah said, were of ex­treme con­cen­tra­tion and focus. You need the din of the world to col­lect dots, Varma said, and still­ness to let them soak in.
## What ef­fort builds
John Collison, a founder of Stripe, wrote that the world is a mu­seum of pas­sion projects. Shah added an old Turkish proverb: a for­est takes a hun­dred years to grow and one night to burn.
Paul Graham’s arith­metic, that most of the best peo­ple at any­thing are born abroad, be­came a case for in­ter­na­tional teams. Growth mat­ters, Shah said, be­cause India wastes so many Ramanujans.
Dharmesh’s call to be an im­per­fec­tion­ist drew Varma’s case for a bias for ac­tion, and Shah’s con­di­tion: ship your gen­uine best, and learn the prin­ci­ple be­hind every cor­rec­tion.
The body­builder Ronnie Coleman sup­plied the bluntest line: “Everybody wants to be a body­builder, but no­body wants to lift no heavy ass weights.” {#coleman}
Varma used it to sep­a­rate thin de­sires, copied from oth­ers, from thick ones, loved for the work it­self. People with thin de­sires, he said, won’t put in the hard yards.
## When com­fort be­comes the prob­lem

Anthony Bourdain wrote of a lazy guy in his head. Varma’s, he con­fessed, prac­ti­cally dwarfs him. Shah, a self-described junkie, has never felt the con­flict. “Find pur­pose, the rest will fol­low,” is his motto. {094-C19}

Sahil Bloom’s tweet, that there is no such thing as mak­ing it, left Varma wor­ried about com­pla­cency, his own in­cluded. Shah found it too bleak. The real prob­lem, he said, is short-termism: many of their view­ers work hard but take too few risks.
Gurwinder Bhogal warned that the fu­ture is con­stantly shrink­ing. Shah’s an­swer to vague angst about the world was to be self­ish: ask what you will read, write and do to­mor­row.
The last tweet was from Frog and Toad, in which Frog’s fa­ther prom­ises that spring is just around the cor­ner. Things get bet­ter, Varma said, but only when you do things. {094-C23}
“We each of us have to wake up and do things,” Shah said.

Shah then ad­mit­ted he had come with­out his promised seven rec­om­men­da­tions, so Varma drafted the crew, who were, he said, “truly beau­ti­ful, in­side and out­side”. “The good Lord put the ugly one in front of the cam­era.”

second.label: Isaac Newton
second.head: The moon could wait
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why greatness is quiet concentration, not a frantic sprint

pic.caption: Isaac Newton, painted by Godfrey Kneller in 1689

body: Isaac Newton, Ajay Shah said, al­ready had pretty much all the right ideas when he made a rough cal­cu­la­tion of the moon’s pe­riod. It came out about ten or fif­teen per cent off. {094-S06}
Newton con­cluded he was wrong, and sat qui­etly. Months and years later, bet­ter con­stants reached him, the pieces of the puz­zle clicked, and he saw that he had been right all along.

“I would not fetish the sprint,” Shah said, re­ject­ing startup culture’s adren­a­line-laced hard work. {#sprint} The lives of Newton and Einstein, he said, were lives of ex­treme con­cen­tra­tion and focus, pas­sion­ate about per­fec­tion­ism.

quote.text: Newton con­cluded, Okay, so I’m wrong. And he sat qui­etly.

third.head: Master turned bug tester

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the bug tester

body: Ajay Shah will point out a kind of mis­take to a young col­league once, twice or thrice. By the fifth or sixth time, he won­ders if they are even notic­ing.
Then, he said, he has be­come somebody’s bug tester: he finds the mis­takes in shoddy code or a bad doc­u­ment, and “like a cler­i­cal func­tion” they get fixed. No les­son sticks.
He looks for a thirst for ex­cel­lence: ship your gen­uine best, and ask of every cor­rec­tion what the gen­eral prin­ci­ple is. Otherwise you are a typ­ist fix­ing a typo.

“Then you have turned your skilled mas­ter into your bug tester, which is a waste of life,” Shah said. {094-S09} Amit Varma added that peo­ple who use a men­tor as a crutch, not a tool, are ex­actly the kind AI will re­place. {094-C16}

p2.title: The gyan folder
p2.deck: Amit Varma keeps many hundreds of tweets in a Good Gyan folder. Twelve made the cut. {#folder}

quote.text: If you re­ally want to do some­thing, go out there, get the job done.

box.title: Where the gyan came from
box.text: The twelve came from Twitter: John Coltrane, Greg Isenberg, Tiago Forte, Brene Brown via Polina Pompliano, John Collison, Paul Graham, Dharmesh, Ronnie Coleman, Anthony Bourdain, Sahil Bloom, Gurwinder Bhogal and Frog and Toad. Amit Varma urged view­ers to fol­low such ac­counts. {094-R17}

sections.label: Good Gyan One
sections.head: No Fender, no excuse
sections.caption: playing a shoestring
body: John Coltrane said you can play a shoe­string if you’re sin­cere. Amit Varma loves the line be­cause of the ex­cuses it an­swers. {094-C01}

People tell him they want to learn the gui­tar but can­not af­ford a Fender, or want to start a YouTube show but have only a phone cam­era, “not even an iPhone”. His reply: none of that mat­ters. William Shakespeare, he said, found a quill from some­where and got the job done.
Coltrane had earned the intro: the hosts’ friend Shruti Rajagopalan, a huge fan, named her two dogs Cole and Train.
## Learning on air
The hosts’ own show was Varma’s ex­am­ple. Neither of them knew any­thing about YouTube when they started, he said, “but we jumped into it and I think we did great.”
Ajay Shah, with the show ap­proach­ing its hun­dredth episode, said he was “as­ton­ished and happy be­yond my wildest dreams”. {#youtube}

Conventional mass media, he said, chases vol­ume and does not push this kind of ex­otic con­tent. Once, the BBC had to com­mis­sion Jacob Bronowski’s *The Ascent of Man*; now YouTube lets two peo­ple build “a lot of time­less ma­te­rial” for “a tiny cadre of crazy peo­ple all over the coun­try, all over the world”.

~ Shah later added his own list of ex­cuses to ig­nore: no in­vi­ta­tion to a Rockefeller Foundation cas­tle in Italy, no hun­dred-dollar pen. You can read and think, he said, on the floor of an Indian sec­ond-class train. {094-J02}

quote.text: If you re­ally want to do some­thing, go out there, get the job done.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on playing a shoestring

sections.label: Good Gyan Two
sections.head: Happy in shark waters
sections.caption: comfort and greatness
body: Greg Isenberg’s tweet of­fered five words: great­ness and com­fort rarely co­ex­ist. {#greatness} Amit Varma felt leav­ing the com­fort zone was worth it, and ad­mit­ted he did not do it enough.

Ajay Shah’s an­ti­dote, in the realm of ideas, is to index every view on a zero-to-one scale of how sure he is, and of whether it came from au­thor­i­ties or his own rea­son­ing. Enter a new field and every value starts near zero, which holds no ter­ror. {094-C02}
Then, he said, you are swim­ming in shark-infested ter­ri­tory, “and that’s a good place to be”.
## The price of com­fort

Varma saw a trade-off. Time, band­width and en­ergy are lim­ited, and some things in the com­fort zone “we are bloody good at”. If mas­ter­ing a craft takes ten thou­sand hours, should three thou­sand go else­where? {#tenhours}

Perhaps great­ness is “an al­lur­ing false tar­get”, he won­dered, which ar­rives by the way while you live. Shah’s an­swer was prac­ti­cal: you know great­ness only in hind­sight. In the flow, all you can ob­serve is your en­ergy, ex­cite­ment and con­cen­tra­tion. {094-C06}
~ Varma also bor­rowed from Bob Dylan: “He not busy being born is busy dying.” {094-J13}

quote.text: What is worth liv­ing for is a life of the mind, is a jour­ney of the mind.

art.caption: Amit Varma on comfort and greatness

sections.label: Good Gyan Four
sections.head: Grateful for a clear nose
sections.caption: ordinary moments
body: Brene Brown wrote that we chase ex­tra­or­di­nary mo­ments in­stead of being grate­ful for or­di­nary ones, until hard­ship leaves us beg­ging for a nor­mal mo­ment. Amit Varma, who found her words in a tweet by Polina Pompliano, called it beau­ti­ful. {094-R16}
He has lived it. When a bad cold blocks a nos­tril, he thinks of all the days he breathed freely and was not grate­ful.

On an ear­lier shoot at the same lo­ca­tion, he skipped the usual ten-to-fifteen-minute walk be­cause his chest felt con­stricted. That was be­fore his heart at­tack. Now he can come on the walk again. {094-S07}
## Care by cal­en­dar

Varma’s word for what mat­ters is in­ten­tion­al­ity. Tiago Forte’s tweet had listed four kinds of pro­duc­tiv­ity, task, in­tel­lec­tual, emo­tional and so­cial, and Varma said we are in­ten­tional about tasks but rarely about the rest. {#tiago}

Ajay Shah was ner­vous: friend­ships should be spon­ta­neous, not cal­cu­lat­ing. Varma said he meant car­ing, not trans­ac­tional. One friend of theirs meets a new per­son every week, and calls a loved one every sin­gle day. {094-C11}
~ Shah, for his part, re­sisted the word pro­duc­tiv­ity. “Ultimately you need imag­i­na­tion,” he said. {094-C09}

quote.text: Now I can come on the walk. That or­di­nary mo­ment is so im­por­tant.

sections.label: Good Gyan Six
sections.head: No quota for genius
sections.caption: talent born abroad
body: Paul Graham’s tweet of­fered “some very sim­ple math”: if a coun­try has five per cent of the world’s pop­u­la­tion and abil­ity is evenly dis­trib­uted, 95 per cent of the best peo­ple at any­thing will be born abroad. Amit Varma read it as an an­swer to today’s xeno­pho­bia. {094-C13}
Ajay Shah’s case in point was Gukesh’s world-championship team, for which Anand helped find a Polish helper and oth­ers. “There was no Indian quota,” he said. {094-S08}
Indian firms, he ar­gued, should hire ex­plic­itly multi­na­tional work­forces. Not all knowl­edge is in India, and the cul­tural ho­mo­gene­ity of many work­places is an im­ped­i­ment.
## Wider tails
If you are one in a mil­lion, Shah said, there are 1,400 of you in India. The tragedy is how many are wasted: “just think of all the Ramanujans in India who are being wasted”. {094-J17}

Variance, he ar­gued, is cul­tural as well as bi­o­log­i­cal. A so­ci­ety that em­braces mav­er­icks, dis­si­dents and non­con­formists gets more peo­ple in the upper tail; an obe­di­ent one gets a tight dis­tri­bu­tion.
~ Varma took on the case against low-skilled mi­grants. They do jobs lo­cals don’t want, he said, and slums are the entry point to the city for many peo­ple. {#slums}

quote.text: All the good things in the world come from that hand­ful of upper tails.

art.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on talent born abroad, with Amit Varma

sections.label: Good Gyan Seven
sections.head: Imperfect, and proud of it
sections.caption: being an imperfectionist
body: Dharmesh’s tweet said im­per­fec­tion­ists hit pub­lish, ship prod­uct and it­er­ate pub­licly: “They dream big, but it­er­ate small.” Amit Varma called it al­most the mantra of his life. {094-R19}

He tells writ­ing stu­dents that per­fec­tion is the enemy of pro­duc­tion. Whatever you start, you suck at first, and you get good only by doing. His ad­vice: own the suck­i­ness. He ad­mits he preaches it more than he prac­tises it: “I should have writ­ten ten books by now.”
Ajay Shah said this way of think­ing came to him from Varma. He agreed on vol­ume, but wanted every piece shipped as best you know.
## Thinking, not dawdling

Shah con­fessed to two stages of pro­cras­ti­na­tion. The first, mulling a prob­lem until the pieces click, he no longer counts as pro­cras­ti­na­tion. Varma had a name for it: “The Bengali word for it is mar­i­na­tion.” {094-J05}

The sec­ond is per­fec­tion­ist ter­ror of the idea that ar­rives too late. His fix comes from big soft­ware projects, which plot new bugs found per day and ship once the count has held at zero for a cou­ple of days. {#bugcurve}
~ Varma con­ceded that his own slo­gan risks a false bi­nary. “Perfection is achieved only through con­stant pro­duc­tion,” he said. {094-C15}

quote.text: At this point I’ve stopped call­ing it pro­cras­ti­na­tion. I think I was ac­tu­ally think­ing.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on being an imperfectionist

sections.label: Good Gyan Ten
sections.head: The lion has a freezer
sections.caption: comfort and complacency
body: Sahil Bloom’s tweet told the old story of the sa­van­nah: every morn­ing the gazelle must out­run the lion, and the lion the gazelle. There is no such thing as mak­ing it, he wrote; Apple must keep mak­ing iPhones. {094-R22}

Amit Varma agreed that com­pla­cency, a side ef­fect of pros­per­ity, is a great dan­ger. Then he up­dated the para­ble: today’s lion can store gazelles in the freezer, and the gazelle can live in a gated so­ci­ety. “Like no one should be eaten.” {094-J08}
Ajay Shah found the tweet “too bleak by half”, a “life is short, nasty, and brutish view of the world”. {094-J18}
## Risk, not grind

Most of us have more space than that, he said. The real choke points are short-termism and chas­ing likes in­stead of gen­uine thought. “I think a lot of EIE view­ers are worka­holic, but not enough risk is present in their lives and in their worlds.” {094-C20}

Gurwinder Bhogal’s tweet raised the stakes. Varma’s ex­er­cise for any­one in their thir­ties liv­ing away from their par­ents: make an op­ti­mistic guess of their life­span and of how often you will see them each year. The total is not a lot. {#parents}
~ Shah’s ad­vice was to be self­ish: you con­trol only what you do, and a very good you cre­ates pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­i­ties for ev­ery­one around you.

quote.text: Your fu­ture is con­stantly shrink­ing. So the longer you spend pre­par­ing for it, the smaller it’s going to be.
quote.who: Gurwinder Bhogal, as read by Amit Varma

art.caption: Amit Varma (right) on comfort and complacency, with Ajay Shah

quote.text: Spring does not come on its own. Perhaps spring is al­ready there and you just have to look in­side your mind to find it. But your ac­tions also mat­ter.

p3.title: Told along the way
p3.deck: A father’s gift, a poker bottle, a king of typos and a worrying comfort

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the path his father set
stories.head: A gift from his father
body: Early in the episode, after ask­ing how he felt about their YouTube jour­ney, Amit Varma put a sec­ond ques­tion to Ajay Shah. Set aside whether he got into a uni­ver­sity to study it, or lived in a big city among like-minded peo­ple: what would he have done no mat­ter what?

Shah said he did not know how to think about his life with­out all of its cul­tural con­text. He re­minded Varma of the “ridicu­lous ten and a half hour con­ver­sa­tion about my life” the two had once recorded. {#tenhalf}
“I feel like I’m just com­pletely tied to that tra­jec­tory,” he said. He grew up with his fa­ther, and with an in­ter­est in the world, “and that was ev­ery­thing”.
His fa­ther died when he was sev­en­teen. “But I got that in­ter­est in the world from him,” Shah said, “and I don’t know how to think about it any other way.” {#seventeen}
Once that in­ter­est was in place, he said, he did not need the lux­ury of money and re­sources, books and uni­ver­si­ties. “I would have just pow­ered and done it.”

Then came a con­fes­sion. “I have three great re­grets in my life,” he said. He does not know how to play a mu­si­cal in­stru­ment. He wishes he knew maths, “re­ally se­ri­ously”. And he wishes he knew more bi­ol­ogy. {094-S01}
~ Varma did not linger. His next tweet, by Greg Isenberg, was about great­ness and com­fort, and how rarely the two co­ex­ist.
stories.why: Shah’s cu­rios­ity, in his telling, was in­her­ited rather than cho­sen, and once he had it, noth­ing could have stopped him. Yet even a mind that keeps start­ing new fields car­ries a short list of roads not taken.
stories.postscript: Later, Nomsita Haritashya turned his first re­gret into a rec­om­men­da­tion: pick up a mu­si­cal in­stru­ment, if you have even two per cent of the willpower. {094-R12}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father and three regrets

stories.kicker: Amit Varma remembers his professional poker days
stories.head: Fifteen tables and a bottle
body: Nomsita Haritashya, who edits the show, had a ques­tion from be­hind the cam­era. Pop cul­ture shows great­ness as dis­com­fort: long hours, no sleep, a pro­tein bar in­stead of a meal. How should a young per­son read that?
Amit Varma said the pic­ture was both true and false. Excellence takes hard work, but burn­ing your­self out is not the only path to great­ness.

He re­mem­bered his pro­fes­sional poker days. Some play­ers multi-tabled fif­teen ta­bles at a time, “and they’d ac­tu­ally keep a bot­tle with them be­cause they wouldn’t want to get up to go pee”. {094-S05} “I think that kind of thing is just crazy,” he said.
~ His coun­ter­weight was Cal Newport’s *Slow Productivity*, which he read on a flight: let ideas mar­i­nate in a quiet life. {094-R01}
stories.why: Hard work mat­ters, but grind is not the whole of it. You need the din of the world to col­lect dots, Varma said, and the still­ness of *thehrav* and *sukoon* to let them soak in. {094-C07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the poker grinders

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on publishing, mistakes and all
stories.head: Read twice, then publish
body: Amit Varma calls him­self the king of typos. He has writ­ten hun­dreds of col­umns and, in blog­ging days that ended fif­teen years ago, “lit­er­ally many thou­sands of posts”.
Avoiding typos, he said, would be im­pos­si­ble for him. So his method is sim­ple: write, read it over once, read it over twice, and pub­lish.
“And I will al­ways miss a typo,” he said. “But al­ways, al­ways, al­ways. Within a cou­ple of days no typos exist on that page be­cause read­ers have writ­ten to me.” {094-S10}
~ They write to say he did this or did that, “so that helps”. It was his reply to Ajay Shah’s bug curve: in his case, he said, the bugs never go to zero.
stories.why: Shipping and let­ting read­ers help with the fixes beats end­less pri­vate pol­ish­ing. It is the im­per­fec­tion­ist creed that Varma calls al­most the mantra of his life, and preaches to his writ­ing stu­dents even when he falls short. {094-R19}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the king of typos

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the risk of feeling comfortable
stories.head: Too comfortable for comfort
body: Sahil Bloom’s tweet, that there is no such thing as mak­ing it, sent Amit Varma back to an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Roshan Abbas. {094-R33}
Varma had asked him about FU money and FO money. Abbas said he had FU money, but not FO money. He gave fig­ures for both, Varma re­called, and “they’re both in­sane”.
“I’m far from both of them,” Varma said. “But I’m com­fort­able. And that com­fort kinda wor­ries me.” {094-S11}

~ Prosperity is in­cred­i­ble, he said, but one of its side ef­fects is com­pla­cency: it is not that hard to get pros­per­ous enough to lose the hunger, to feel you have achieved what you set out to.
stories.why: Comfort can qui­etly dis­solve the hunger that earned it, Varma warned. Ajay Shah thought most peo­ple have more room than the lion-and-gazelle story al­lows, and need more risk in their lives rather than more grind.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 94. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: John Coltrane (Gelderen, Hugo van / Anefo, CC0); Isaac Newton (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Brené Brown (Dell Inc., CC BY 2.0); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain); Srinivasa Ramanujan (Konrad Jacobs, public domain); Martin Scorsese (Montclair Film, CC BY 2.0); Wim Wenders (Martin Kraft, CC BY-SA 3.0); Richard Linklater (Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0).

shelf.title: Slow Productivity
shelf.creator: Cal Newport
shelf.why: It ar­gues you don’t need a con­stant mad sprint.

shelf.title: Wanting
shelf.creator: Luke Burgis
shelf.why: Burgis brings René Girard’s mimetic de­sire into ev­ery­day life: we want things be­cause oth­ers want them.

shelf.title: Four Thousand Weeks
shelf.creator: Oliver Burkeman
shelf.why: It makes you reckon with how lit­tle time a life ac­tu­ally holds, which works as a spur to act now rather than keep pre­par­ing.

shelf.title: Life Lessons (Scorsese’s segment of New York Stories)
shelf.creator: Martin Scorsese
shelf.why: Amit calls Scorsese’s short a mas­ter­piece whose scenes still play in his head.

shelf.title: The Last Waltz
shelf.creator: Martin Scorsese
shelf.why: In the late 1970s The Band, often Dylan’s back­ing band on tour, de­cided to re­tire after one last con­cert and in­vited friends to per­form, in­clud­ing Dylan and Van Morrison (Amit’s favourite).

shelf.title: Roger Ebert’s review of New York Stories
shelf.creator: Roger Ebert
shelf.why: A com­pan­ion read to the short film that named their course.

shelf.title: Waking Life (and Richard Linklater’s whole filmography)
shelf.creator: Richard Linklater
shelf.why: Vaishnav feels Linklater cap­tures the essence of life.

shelf.title: Solitude
shelf.why: Spend time with your­self and think about life.

shelf.title: Red Dead Redemption 2
shelf.creator: Rockstar Games
shelf.why: It is a slow, peace­ful game with a thick story, his­tory it gets right, thick char­ac­ters, well-written di­a­logue and strong act­ing.

shelf.title: Perfect Days
shelf.creator: Wim Wenders
shelf.why: Wenders’s film pairs the striv­ing of sim­ply being at your work with mo­ments of si­lence and soli­tude we rarely get; Amit calls it ‘a film that could only be made by an old man’.

shelf.title: Rolling Thunder Review
shelf.creator: Martin Scorsese
shelf.why: It cap­tures the hunger the hosts keep de­scrib­ing: to get to some­thing, to do some­thing, and to do it with the peo­ple you love.

shelf.title: Pick up a musical instrument
shelf.why: If you have even two per­cent of the willpower, do it.

shelf.title: John Coltrane on desire
shelf.creator: John Coltrane
shelf.why: Amit’s an­swer to peo­ple who say they lack the gear or re­sources to pur­sue what they love.

shelf.title: Greg Isenberg on greatness
shelf.creator: Greg Isenberg
shelf.why: It prompted a dis­cus­sion of when to stay in your com­fort zone and when to leave it.

shelf.title: Tiago Forte on productivity
shelf.creator: Tiago Forte
shelf.why: A cor­rec­tive to treat­ing pro­duc­tiv­ity as noth­ing but tick­ing off tasks.

shelf.title: Polina Pompliano quoting Brene Brown on normalcy
shelf.creator: Brene Brown (via Polina Pompliano)
shelf.why: Amit finds it beau­ti­ful and lives it: a blocked nos­tril, or a walk he couldn’t take be­fore his heart at­tack, re­minds him to value nor­malcy.

shelf.title: John Collison on passion
shelf.creator: John Collison
shelf.why: It blew Amit’s mind.

shelf.title: Paul Graham on talent
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: A sharp an­swer to today’s xeno­pho­bia and anti-immigrant sen­ti­ment.

shelf.title: Dharmesh on imperfectionism
shelf.creator: Dharmesh
shelf.why: Amit calls it al­most the mantra of his life, the same thing he tells his writ­ing stu­dents.

shelf.title: Rollo Tomassi quoting Ronnie Coleman on the hard yards
shelf.creator: Ronnie Coleman (via Rollo Tomassi)
shelf.why: Aspiration means noth­ing with­out the work.

shelf.title: Anthony Bourdain on procrastination
shelf.creator: Anthony Bourdain
shelf.why: It de­scribes Amit’s own daily strug­gle with the lazy self who wants to play on­line chess and binge YouTube.

shelf.title: Sahil Bloom on making it
shelf.creator: Sahil Bloom
shelf.why: It res­onated as a warn­ing against the com­pla­cency that pros­per­ity breeds.

shelf.title: Gurwinder Bhogal on our shrinking future
shelf.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
shelf.why: Amit reads it as a call to ac­tion and calls Gurwinder a fount of wis­dom.

shelf.title: Frog and Toad on spring
shelf.creator: Arnold Lobel (via the Frog and Toad Bot)
shelf.why: A gen­tle re­minder for any­one in dark times to zoom out, and to act.

shelf.title: Good Gyan 1 (Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: More wis­dom gath­ered from so­cial media in the same for­mat.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: Rules, Not Discretion (Episode 92, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why a good so­ci­ety is built on rules rather than dis­cre­tionary power, which can’t an­chor long-term in­vest­ment, and why ex­perts should stay scep­ti­cal of their own ex­per­tise.

shelf.title: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Episode 323, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah & Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: Ajay and Mohit Satyanand on the SVB col­lapse and bank­ing fun­da­men­tals, in­clud­ing the coun­ter­in­tu­itive case that bank fail­ures are part of a healthy sys­tem, and how elec­tronic pay­ments let a bank’s money flee over a week­end.

shelf.title: The Heart of Disruption (Episode 86, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why big com­pa­nies crum­ble when they can’t adapt and how some es­cape that fate, told through Netflix’s 2007 stream­ing bet and the first half of Amit’s own startup saga.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: Luke Burgis Sees the Deer at His Window (Episode 337, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A fuller treat­ment of mimetic de­sire and why some wants are bor­rowed.

shelf.title: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye & Roshan Abbas
shelf.why: Amit’s adda with friends Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, the source of sto­ries he keeps re­turn­ing to: the friend who changed his mind about liv­ing long, healthy lives, and tal­ented small-town kids los­ing their depth in Bombay, a re­minder that clus­ters can cor­rupt as well as up­lift.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Ajay ar­rived with­out his promised seven rec­om­men­da­tions, so Amit drafted the crew. ‘Two of them are truly beau­ti­ful, in­side and out­side. And you put them be­hind the cam­era. The good Lord put the ugly one in front of the cam­era.’

On Ajay’s bro­ken prom­ise to watch one film a month: ‘I’ll watch movies thor­oughly when you turn cart­wheels on the floor.’ Amit: ‘Bro, if I try to turn cart­wheels on the floor, I could get an­other heart at­tack. You can watch movies with­out any dan­ger to your health. Kindly con­sider.’
Amit on Bourdain’s lazy inner guy: his own is so huge ‘he prac­ti­cally dwarfs me... you could say this guy is me and I am sub­sidiary to him.’
Bob Dylan, ‘He not busy being born is busy dying’, and Annie Dillard, ‘how we spend our days is how we spend our lives’, both quoted by Amit on com­fort zones and great­ness.
Ramanujan: ‘just think of all the Ramanujans in India who are being wasted’. Ajay notes the one who was found died early, partly from the pri­va­tion of his early years.

entries.clue: Jazz great, his name shared by two dogs
Use AI as a tool, never as this
The world is one of passion projects
Champion whose team had no Indian quota
Savannah runner who can now use a freezer
India wastes many of these, said Shah
He sat quietly when the moon didn’t add up
What Coltrane said you can play if sincere
Calm in which ideas soak in
A hundred years to grow, a night to burn
What the careless junior turns the master into
Kept by grinders who wouldn’t leave to pee
Just around the corner, said Frog’s father
